title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
Scammers used AI to create a fake interview article featuring real people, ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock, discussing a cryptocurrency platform. The article never happened, but it was designed to appear credible enough to deceive investors into trusting the unlicensed platform. This is an impersonation attack where AI made fabricated content convincing and difficult to distinguish from real journalism.

The system that failed is the content ecosystem itself. No verification step existed between the creation of the fake article and its circulation to potential victims. Catching this would have required either independent verification of the interview before publication, or alerts to consumers that they should verify credentials through official channels rather than trusting polished-looking content featuring familiar figures.

ASIC reports that similar schemes are increasing rapidly as AI makes fraudulent impersonations easier to produce at scale. It is not established whether any particular AI system was deployed for this purpose, only that AI-generated deepfakes and fabricated content are being used in this class of scam. The fake article exemplifies how systems built to generate plausible text can be used outside their intended purpose, to defraud rather than to inform.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake interview article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has highlighted a growing scam trend in Australia. The fabricated article portrayed an increasingly tense discussion about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fake interview never occurred, yet it exemplifies how scammers use AI-generated deepfakes and fabricated content to deceive investors. ASIC reports this type of scheme is rapidly increasing as artificial intelligence makes fraudulent content more convincing and difficult to detect.

ASIC's latest research reveals significant growth in investment scams, with the regulator removing 19,400 schemes last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scam removals jumped 279 percent while fake investment platforms surged 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of commonly impersonated public figures, alongside other politicians and business leaders including Alan Kohler, Dick Smith, and Gina Rinehart. ASIC warns consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers independently and advises that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy. The regulator is increasing enforcement efforts while encouraging investors to thoroughly check company credentials before investing.
